053219edcee96ecd.text: Check before you share. Every post is made by someone, for a reason. Some want to inform you. Some want to sell to you. Some want to make you angry, scared or excited — because angry, scared and excited people share. Start by sorting what you're reading: A fact can be checked: “The game starts at 7pm.” An opinion is what someone thinks: “It'll be the best game of the year.” A feeling is how someone feels: “I'm so excited!” Fake posts mix these up. They use loaded words — shocking, banned, they don't want you to know — to make an opinion feel like a fact. Fair, objective writing sticks to facts. Subjective writing is full of feelings and opinions. Photos and videos can be faked too. AI tools can now make a realistic picture of anyone, doing anything. So before you share, use SIFT: Stop. Investigate the source. Find better coverage. Trace it back to where it started.

8ab5db7325a4e2cc.text: The puffer-jacket Pope. In March 2023, an image of Pope Francis wearing a long white puffer jacket appeared online. It looked like a real photo. It was shared all over Twitter and TikTok, and many people believed it. It wasn't real. Fact-checkers found it had been made with an AI image tool called Midjourney and first posted on Reddit. NBC News called it one of the first times AI-made misinformation spread on a huge scale. Clues were there — blurry hands, odd details — but most people didn't look closely before sharing. Think about it. How was the image made, and where was it first posted? Why do you think so many people believed it? What clues could have given it away?

1f554e8244e20604.text: Australia's fact-checkers. AAP FactCheck is a team at Australian Associated Press. AAP is a national news agency. The team checks claims that spread online. It checks social media posts, viral videos and what public figures say. First it looks for where a claim came from. Then it asks experts. It also checks what other trusted sources say. Then it shares what it found, with a verdict such as False or Misleading. You can do the same steps yourself. It only takes a few minutes. Think about it. What steps does AAP FactCheck take? Which of those steps could you do on your phone?

06dd18b8640b0688.text: Check before you share. Every post is made by someone, for a reason. Some want to inform you. Some want to sell to you. Some want to make you angry, scared or excited — because emotional people share. Start by sorting what you're reading: A fact can be checked: “The game starts at 7pm.” An opinion is what someone thinks: “It'll be the best game of the year.” A feeling is how someone feels: “I'm so excited!” Fake or slanted posts blur these. They use loaded language — shocking, banned, they don't want you to know — to dress an opinion up as a fact. Objective writing sticks to evidence; subjective writing is coloured by feelings and opinions. Even real news can show bias through what it includes, leaves out, or which quotes it picks. Context matters too. A post reflects when and why it was made: the puffer-jacket Pope spread in 2023, the year AI image tools went mainstream and most people didn't yet know what they could do. Before you share, use SIFT: Stop. Investigate the source. Find better coverage. Trace claims, quotes and images back to where they started.
